content: Testing for HIV is critical to reducing disease progression and preventing further viral transmission. Beyond the test-and-treat approach, programs aim to connect HIV-positive individuals to socioeconomic welfare schemes and improve access to services for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), HIV, and reproductive health, particularly among female partners of men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender populations. The Sahay project employs diverse, community-specific strategies, such as setting up community-based testing sites in underserved areas like mines, mills, factories, construction sites, social gatherings, and migration hubs. It also utilizes smartphone applications, SMS-based platforms, and online social networks to reach lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) populations. Between November 2017 and September 2018, over 36,000 individuals were tested at 717 sites, with 22% testing positive and 91% of those linked to antiretroviral therapy (ART). The Samarth project in India focuses on strengthening the test-treat-adhere-prevent cascade for MSM, transgender, and hijra populations. It is a community-led HIV screening initiative that aligns with India's need for evidence-based interventions. The program has demonstrated effective mobilization strategies, reaching individuals who had never been tested before and linking 80% of those with reactive results to free ART services. The program has also contributed to the development of community-based screening guidelines for national implementation. Faith-based initiatives in Uganda have leveraged local churches to increase demand for HIV services. Faith leaders and volunteers were trained to provide HIV information, referrals, and record-keeping. Health kiosks at worship centers served as entry points for HIV services, linking those who tested positive to care and treatment while connecting those who tested negative to prevention services. Collaboration with the Ministry of Health and local health facilities strengthened service linkages, and the use of locally available information materials ensured regular access to HIV education. The HIV/AIDS and Health Initiatives in Workplaces Activity (HIWA) in Uganda, funded by USAID, scaled up comprehensive HIV/AIDS services for workers and their families across 50 districts. A 24/7 call center staffed by medical professionals provided health information, counseling, and referrals. The program also delivered direct services and technical assistance to health facilities, with 97% of referred clients completing the referral process and 83% of those diagnosed with HIV linked to treatment. One Tent Health in Washington, D.C., offers rapid HIV screening in community hubs like grocery stores and laundromats, targeting high-prevalence neighborhoods. Services are free and accessible, with results provided in 15 minutes or less. Those testing positive are linked to care, while those testing negative are connected to prevention services, including condoms and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). The program collaborates with local health facilities and social networking platforms to publicize services and improve access to HIV testing. The Sisli Health Clinic in Istanbul, Turkey, integrates HIV education, prevention, testing, and counseling into primary health services, providing care without stigma or discrimination. The clinic is funded by municipal taxes and offers services at no additional cost. It serves as a model for community-based HIV care, particularly for LGBT and refugee populations, and has strong ties with community-based organizations. The clinic uses an electronic coding system to maintain client confidentiality and track care outcomes. The Zindagi project in Pakistan provides harm reduction services to approximately 20,000 street-based drug users annually across 30 districts. Recognizing the vulnerability of spouses and intimate partners of drug users, the program offers HIV testing, counseling, safer sex education, nutritional support, and linkage to care. Female outreach workers conduct home visits and register spouses in the program, ensuring comprehensive HIV prevention and care services.
